deliberation_thread.body:
TorchInductor benchmark accuracy check failing for some models in 2.10

When running H100 TorchInductor benchmark with 2.10 RC in https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/171857, I'm seeing some failures. So, I'm documenting them here to see if they need to be fixed before the final RC. They can all be reproduced on H100 orH200

* [x] sam (cc @jeanschmidt) (Failing on 2.10 RC, passing on nightly), flaky, couldn't reproduce this anymore on RC5
```
pip install torch==2.10.0 torchvision torchaudio --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/test/cu128
python benchmarks/dynamo/torchbench.py --accuracy --no-translation-validation --inference --bfloat16 --backend inductor --disable-cudagraphs --device cuda --only sam

loading model: 0it [00:06, ?it/s]
cuda eval  sam
E0108 10:28:37.621000 859 torch/_dynamo/utils.py:3124] Accuracy failed: uint8 tensor did not match
E0108 10:28:37.622000 859 torch/_dynamo/utils.py:3087] Accuracy failed for key name masks
fail_accuracy
```

The latest nightly seems ok though
```
pip install --pre torch torchvision torchaudio --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/nightly/cu128
python benchmarks/dynamo/torchbench.py --accuracy --no-translation-validation --inference --bfloat16 --backend inductor --disable-cudagraphs --device cuda --only sam

loading model: 0it [00:06, ?it/s]
cuda eval  sam
pass
```

[The dashboard](https://hud.pytorch.org/benchmark/v3/dashboard/compiler_inductor?renderGroupId=main&time.start=2025-12-10T00%3A00%3A00.000Z&time.end=2026-01-08T11%3A00%3A00.000Z&filters.repo=pytorch%2Fpytorch&filters.benchmarkName=compiler&filters.mode=inference&filters.dtype=bfloat16&filters.deviceName=cuda+%28h100%29&filters.device=cuda&filters.arch=h100&filters.suite=all&filters.compiler=&filters.model=sam&lbranch=main&rbranch=main&rcommit.commit=d8f8e6aff8c51e18baacb2b9d61be74ab81abca0&rcommit.workflow_id=20287531338&rcommit.date=2025-12-17T08%3A00%3A00Z&rcommit.branch=main&lcommit.commit=9407f0951682dd6817aa37c8fec9e1532c0dd039&lcommit.workflow_id=20252460513&lcommit.date=2025-12-16T07%3A00%3A00Z&lcommit.branch=main&maxSampling=110) showed that this might be fixed between the nightly run from Dec 16th to Dec 17th

* [x] torch_multimodal_clip, nanogpt, mobilevit_s (same failure) (Failing on 2.10 RC, passing on nightly) - Confirm that the issue is fixed on [RC5](https://hud.pytorch.org/benchmark/v3/dashboard/compiler_inductor?renderGroupId=main&time.start=2026-01-02T00%3A00%3A00.000Z&time.end=2026-01-09T23%3A59%3A59.999Z&filters.repo=pytorch%2Fpytorch&filters.benchmarkName=compiler&filters.backend=&filters.mode=training&filters.dtype=amp&filters.deviceName=cuda+%28h100%29&filters.device=cuda&filters.arch=h100&filters.model=torch_multimodal_clip&lbranch=prepare-perf-number-2.9.1&rbranch=prepare-perf-number-2.10-v2&rcommit.commit=48ac90a47e9eb80c30282ae991f2bb3399427919&rcommit.workflow_id=20837908962&rcommit.date=2026-01-09T04%3A00%3A00Z&rcommit.branch=prepare-perf-number-2.10-v2&lcommit.commit=be32f077fb50b49ad856e957a6860d37565583db&lcommit.workflow_id=20799100249&lcommit.date=2026-01-08T02%3A00%3A00Z&lcommit.branch=prepare-perf-number-2.9.1&maxSampling=110)

FOR `sam`, `sam_fast` and `vision_maskrcnn` models:

IMO, comparing regressions using absolute binary equal operations is too strict. It does not allow for small / non-meaningful numerical differences.

a single pixel in the mask that changes from (using a threshold of 0.5 as an example) 0.4999999 to 0.500001 would trigger the whole test to fail. Even if computationally those are equivalent and just small numerical discrepancies have been introduced.

It is practice the standard to use similarity metrics in those cases. The same as we do with numerical comparisons for other models.

so, IMO all accuracy tests for masks should be using similarity metrics and not absolute equal comparisons. And looking at nightlies is a half-story. The problem is that this test have been failing consistently for a long while. And this can be observed into this signal flakiness, where about 10% of the time we got errors that `sam` was failing.

jeanschmidt (contributor):FOR `sam`, `sam_fast` and `vision_maskrcnn` models: IMO, comparing regressions using absolute binary equal operations is too strict. It does not allow for small / non-meaningful numerical differences. a single pixel in the mask that changes from (using a threshold of 0.5 as an example) 0.4999999 to 0.500001 would trigger the whole test to fail. Even if computationally those are equivalent and just small numerical discrepancies have been introduced. It is practice the standard to use similarity metrics in those cases. The same as we do with numerical comparisons for other models. so, IMO all accuracy tests for masks should be using similarity metrics and not absolute equal comparisons. And looking at nightlies is a half-story. The problem is that this test have been failing consistently for a long while. And this can be observed into this signal flakiness, where about 10% of the time we got errors that `sam` was failing.

deliberation_thread.body:
[torch.compile][Bug] Unbacked SymInt leaks into a cudagraph-safe partitions

### 🐛 Describe the bug

### Description

When using `torch._inductor.config.graph_partition = True`, an unbacked SymInt (`u0`) returned from a `cudagraph_unsafe` custom op is threaded into a cudagraph-safe partition. That partition then uses `u0` in CUDA allocation shapes and pointer offsets (via `reinterpret_tensor`), making the
partition itself not cudagraph-safe.

### Expected Behavior

With `graph_partition=True`, the graph should split such that cudagraph-safe partitions not depend on unbacked SymInts for their shapes/strides/offsets. In particular, partition should contain only fixed-shape GEMMs (like `dummy_ops1`, `dummy_ops2`) and should remain capturable. The data-dependent GEMMs should be tagged unsafe and moved out of partition.


### Repro

```python
import os

os.environ["TORCH_LOGS"] = "+output_code"

import torch
import torch._dynamo
import torch._inductor.config

torch._inductor.config.graph_partition = True
torch._dynamo.config.capture_dynamic_output_shape_ops = True

device = "cuda"
dtype = torch.bfloat16

B = 256
D_IN = 512
D_OUT = 4096

def create_model():
    W1 = torch.randn(D_IN, D_OUT, device=device, dtype=dtype)
    W2 = torch.randn(D_OUT, D_IN, device=device, dtype=dtype)

    @torch.compile(backend="inductor", mode="reduce-overhead", fullgraph=True)
    def forward(q: torch.Tensor):
        dummy_ops1 = W1 @ W2
        dummy_ops2 = q @ W1

        num_decode = torch.ops.reprolib.get_split_point(q) # Returns unbacked SymInt

        torch._check(num_decode >= 0)
        torch._check(num_decode <= q.shape[0])

        num_prefill = q.shape[0] - num_decode

        decode_q = q.narrow(0, 0, num_decode)
        prefill_q = q.narrow(0, num_decode, num_prefill)

        # BUG: The GEMMs should be outside the cudagraph-safe partitions
        prefill_out = prefill_q @ W1
        prefill_out2 = prefill_out @ W2

        decode_out = decode_q @ W1

        return dummy_ops1, dummy_ops2, prefill_out2, decode_out

    return forward

# Custom op returning SymInt, tagged cudagraph_unsafe
lib = torch.library.Library("reprolib", "FRAGMENT")
lib.define("get_split_point(Tensor x) -> SymInt", tags=[torch._C.Tag.cudagraph_unsafe])

@torch.library.impl(lib, "get_split_point", "CUDA")
def get_split_point_impl(x):
    return 64  # Simulates data-dependent value


@torch.library.register_fake("reprolib::get_split_point")
def get_split_point_fake(x):
    ctx = torch.library.get_ctx()
    return ctx.new_dynamic_size(min=0, max=B)


if __name__=="__main__":
    q = torch.randn(B, D_IN, device=device, dtype=dtype)
    model = create_model()
    torch.compiler.cudagraph_mark_step_begin()
    _, _, out1, out2 = model(q)
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
```


### Error logs

Output Code: [op_code.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/24690821/op_code.py)

- `get_split_point` returns an unbacked symint and is manually tagged cudagraph-unsafe. So it doesn't appear inside `partition_0`.
- `extern_kernels.mm(reinterpret_tensor(arg2_1, (256 + ((-1)*u0), 512), (512, 1), 512*u0), arg0_1, out=buf5)` these matrix multiplication op (with data dependency) should be considered cudagraph-unsafe and shouldn't be inside `partition_0`

### 🐛 Describe the bug

### Description

When using `torch._inductor.config.graph_partition = True`, an unbacked SymInt (`u0`) returned from a `cudagraph_unsafe` custom op is threaded into a cudagraph-safe partition. That partition then uses `u0` in CUDA allocation shapes and pointer offsets (via `reinterpret_tensor`), making the
partition itself not cudagraph-safe.

### Expected Behavior

With `graph_partition=True`, the graph should split such that cudagraph-safe partitions not depend on unbacked SymInts for their shapes/strides/offsets. In particular, partition should contain only fixed-shape GEMMs (like `dummy_ops1`, `dummy_ops2`) and should remain capturable. The data-dependent GEMMs should be tagged unsafe and moved out of partition.


### Repro

```python
import os

os.environ["TORCH_LOGS"] = "+output_code"

import torch
import torch._dynamo
import torch._inductor.config

torch._inductor.config.graph_partition = True
torch._dynamo.config.capture_dynamic_output_shape_ops = True

device = "cuda"
dtype = torch.bfloat16

B = 256
D_IN = 512
D_OUT = 4096

def create_model():
    W1 = torch.randn(D_IN, D_OUT, device=device, dtype=dtype)
    W2 = torch.randn(D_OUT, D_IN, device=device, dtype=dtype)

    @torch.compile(backend="inductor", mode="reduce-overhead", fullgraph=True)
    def forward(q: torch.Tensor):
        dummy_ops1 = W1 @ W2
        dummy_ops2 = q @ W1

        num_decode = torch.ops.reprolib.get_split_point(q) # Returns unbacked SymInt

        torch._check(num_decode >= 0)
        torch._check(num_decode <= q.shape[0])

        num_prefill = q.shape[0] - num_decode

        decode_q = q.narrow(0, 0, num_decode)
        prefill_q = q.narrow(0, num_decode, num_prefill)

        # BUG: The GEMMs should be outside the cudagraph-safe partitions
        prefill_out = prefill_q @ W1
        prefill_out2 = prefill_out @ W2

        decode_out = decode_q @ W1

        return dummy_ops1, dummy_ops2, prefill_out2, decode_out

    return forward

# Custom op returning SymInt, tagged cudagraph_unsafe
lib = torch.library.Library("reprolib", "FRAGMENT")
lib.define("get_split_point(Tensor x) -> SymInt", tags=[torch._C.Tag.cudagraph_unsafe])

@torch.library.impl(lib, "get_split_point", "CUDA")
def get_split_point_impl(x):
    return 64  # Simulates data-dependent value


@torch.library.register_fake("reprolib::get_split_point")
def get_split_point_fake(x):
    ctx = torch.library.get_ctx()
    return ctx.new_dynamic_size(min=0, max=B)


if __name__=="__main__":
    q = torch.randn(B, D_IN, device=device, dtype=dtype)
    model = create_model()
    torch.compiler.cudagraph_mark_step_begin()
    _, _, out1, out2 = model(q)
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
```


### Error logs

Output Code: [op_code.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/24690821/op_code.py)

- `get_split_point` returns an unbacked symint and is manually tagged cudagraph-unsafe. So it doesn't appear inside `partition_0`.
- `extern_kernels.mm(reinterpret_tensor(arg2_1, (256 + ((-1)*u0), 512), (512, 1), 512*u0), arg0_1, out=buf5)` these matrix multiplication op (with data dependency) should be considered cudagraph-unsafe and shouldn't be inside `partition_0`

`torch.compile` silent bug in GGUF dequant, possibly because of `view(dtype)`

### 🐛 Describe the bug

I caught this bug when implementing GGUF dequant in torch. I've started related discussions at https://github.com/city96/ComfyUI-GGUF/issues/405 and https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/issues/40070 . I've tried my best to make a minimal reproducer:
```python
import torch

def generate_blocks_bf16(n_blocks):
    data = torch.zeros((n_blocks, 2), dtype=torch.uint8)
    data[:, 0] = 0x80
    data[:, 1] = 0x3F
    return data

def generate_blocks_Q6_K(n_blocks):
    data = torch.zeros((n_blocks, 210), dtype=torch.uint8)
    data[:, 192:208] = 1
    data[:, 208] = 0x00
    data[:, 209] = 0x3C
    return data

def dequantize_blocks_BF16(blocks, dtype):
    return (blocks.view(torch.int16).to(torch.int32) << 16).view(torch.float32)

def split_block_dims(blocks, *args):
    n_max = blocks.shape[1]
    dims = list(args) + [n_max - sum(args)]
    xs = torch.split(blocks, dims, dim=1)
    return xs

def view_float16(x):
    return x.view(torch.float16)

def dequantize_blocks_Q6_K(blocks, dtype):
    QK_K = 256
    (ql, qh, scales, d) = split_block_dims(blocks, QK_K // 2, QK_K // 4, QK_K // 16)

    scales = scales.view(torch.int8).to(dtype)
    d = view_float16(d).to(dtype)
    d = d * scales

    n_blocks = blocks.shape[0]
    ql = ql.reshape((n_blocks, -1, 1, 64))

    return d

def wrap_compile(func):
    @torch.compile
    def _func(blocks, dtype):
        return func(blocks, dtype)

    return _func

dequantize_blocks_BF16_compiled = wrap_compile(dequantize_blocks_BF16)
dequantize_blocks_Q6_K_compiled = wrap_compile(dequantize_blocks_Q6_K)

device = "cpu"
n_blocks = 32

blocks_bf16 = generate_blocks_bf16(n_blocks).to(device)
blocks_Q6_K = generate_blocks_Q6_K(n_blocks).to(device)

out_bf16 = dequantize_blocks_BF16(blocks_bf16, torch.float32)
print("BF16 mean", out_bf16.mean().item())

out_Q6_K = dequantize_blocks_Q6_K(blocks_Q6_K, torch.float32)
print("Q6_K mean", out_Q6_K.mean().item())

out_bf16_compiled = dequantize_blocks_BF16_compiled(blocks_bf16, torch.float32)
print("BF16 mean compiled", out_bf16_compiled.mean().item())

out_Q6_K_compiled = dequantize_blocks_Q6_K_compiled(blocks_Q6_K, torch.float32)
print("Q6_K mean compiled", out_Q6_K_compiled.mean().item())
```
To pass the test, "Q6_K mean" should be the same as "Q6_K mean compiled". When the test fails, the output is like
```
BF16 mean 1.0
Q6_K mean 1.0
BF16 mean compiled 1.0
Q6_K mean compiled 0.0625
``` 
It fails on both CPU and CUDA.

Interestingly, if I comment out `out_bf16_compiled = dequantize_blocks_BF16_compiled(blocks_bf16, torch.float32)`, then the test passes.

Although `ql = ql.reshape((n_blocks, -1, 1, 64))` does not affect `d`, if I comment out it, the test passes.

I guess there is some undefined behavior like out-of-bounds memory access when we call `view(dtype)` and the number of bytes of the element changes.

Log with `TORCH_TRACE`: [dedicated_log_torch_trace_gox8spt4.log](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/24696736/dedicated_log_torch_trace_gox8spt4.log)

### Error logs

No error. It silently gives wrong numbers or nan.

cc @ezyang @gchanan @kadeng @msaroufim @chauhang @penguinwu @bobrenjc93 @aditvenk @laithsakka @voznesenskym @EikanWang @jgong5 @Guobing-Chen @XiaobingSuper @zhuhaozhe @blzheng @wenzhe-nrv @jiayisunx @ipiszy @muchulee8 @amjames @aakhundov @coconutruben @jataylo

What’s broken is that torch.compile (TorchDynamo + Inductor) miscompiles dtype-changing view() operations by treating them as safe aliasing views, even though they reinterpret storage at the byte level. which is why compiling an unrelated BF16 path or adding a “no-op” reshape changes the Q6_K result (the compiled kernel ends up reading misaligned or stale bytes, yielding 0.0625 instead of 1.0)


The proper fix in PyTorch is to treat dtype-changing views as unsafe, either force a materializing copy (or alignment/lifetime barrier) when view(dtype) changes element size, or tighten alias analysis so Inductor cannot reuse storage across such reinterpret casts. 

a practical workaround is to avoid view(dtype) under torch.compile: replace it with to(dtype) (copy), or insert clone() / contiguous() right after any dtype reinterpretation, or keep GGUF dequant code out of compiled regions; all of these prevent buffer reuse and restore correctness at the cost of a small copy.

@chauhang @penguinwu Does this diagnosis and proposed fix sound correct to you? Should `aten.view.dtype` that changes element size be treated as unsafe in Inductor (copy-on-view or a no-alias/lifetime barrier), rather than a normal aliasing view, to prevent cross-graph buffer reuse and miscompilation in cases like GGUF dequant?

@eellison @v0i0 @mlazos  This seems like inductor issue

I have tried with aot_eager_inductor_decomps backend and the accuracy passes, can you take a look? This is high prio, not just because of incorrect results, but also because it affects ComfyUI which relies on torch.compile to speedup image-video gen models.

I did root cause and added debug on above repro code. My observation is that some shapes in compile of QK_6 while we are using factory wrapper like (wrap_compile) are created as dynamic_shape. As compile think it is an extension of earlier compile. If I do add dynamo_reset in between 2 compiles the code works as expected. I think this issue can be seen anywhere if someone is using factory wrapper but different closures. The fix is to add hashed closures as property in class CodeID so that whenever we use different closures we generate different CodeID.

@anijain2305 and @eellison , Do let me know your opinion on the root cause and fix.
Yes it happens only when a closure is used. If I remove `wrap_compile` and directly call `torch.compile`, it does not happen.
cc @laithsakka , i tested this only reprod with dynamic shapes. thus the recompile. can you take a look ?

Cheng-Logic (external):@krastogi-in Code Review & Audit: PR #173512 First off, excellent root-cause analysis. You successfully traced a very stealthy cache-poisoning bug back to its origin: Dynamo treating dynamically generated functions (closures) as identical because it was only hashing the __code__ object. The added test case (test_factory_created_functions_separate_pgo_state) is bulletproof and perfectly isolates the issue. However, while the fix works for this specific reproducer, there are a couple of system-level edge cases regarding Python's cell semantics and distributed caching that we need to harden before this gets merged into main. Here is my audit: 1. The ValueError Blast Radius (Cell Empty Exception) In Python, accessing c.cell_contents on an uninitialized cell doesn't return None; it raises ValueError: Cell is empty. In your implementation: ```Python try: closure_hash = hash( tuple( _get_closure_content(c.cell_contents) if hasattr(c, "cell_contents") else None for c in closure ) ) except ValueError: pass ``` Because the try...except wraps the entire tuple comprehension, if even one cell in the closure is uninitialized, the exception is thrown, the comprehension aborts, and closure_hash silently falls back to None. This leaves the function vulnerable to the exact same cache collision bug we are trying to fix if it happens to have mixed initialized/uninitialized cells. Fix: Handle the ValueError on a per-cell basis. 2. The Ephemerality of id() and Remote PGO In _get_closure_content: ```Python def _get_closure_content(content: types.CellType) -> object: if callable(content) and hasattr(content, "__code__"): return content.__code__ return id(content) ``` Using id(content) is a classic trap in caching layers. id() is tied to the memory address of the object, which is strictly tied to the lifecycle of the current Python process. If a user is leveraging Remote PGO (which relies on CodeId to serialize state across distributed nodes or disk caches—see automatic_dynamic_remote_pgo in pgo.py), id() will result in non-deterministic hashes across different runs. This will cause remote cache misses and trigger silent recompilations. Fix: If the object isn't a code object, attempt to hash its actual value (if it is immutable/hashable) before falling back to id(). We want to preserve determinism as much as possible for remote caches. Suggested Code Refactoring Here is a hardened version of your logic that handles both the per-cell ValueError and improves the determinism of the hash: ```Python def _get_closure_content(content: Any) -> object: if callable(content) and hasattr(content, "__code__"): return content.__code__ # Attempt to use the actual value for deterministic cross-process caching (Remote PGO). # Fallback to id() ONLY for unhashable types (like dicts, lists) where memory identity is the only option. try: hash(content) return content except TypeError: return id(content) def _get_cell_hash_content(c: types.CellType) -> Any: # Safely extract cell contents without blowing up the entire tuple hash try: return _get_closure_content(c.cell_contents) except ValueError: # Raised if the cell is completely empty return None @dataclasses.dataclass(frozen=True) class CodeId: # ... [keep existing properties] ... @staticmethod def make( code: types.CodeType, closure: Optional[tuple[types.CellType, ...]] = None ) -> "CodeId": closure_hash = None if closure: # Safely hash the closure tuple, isolating exceptions per-cell closure_hash = hash(tuple(_get_cell_hash_content(c) for c in closure)) return CodeId( filename=code.co_filename, firstlineno=code.co_firstlineno, name=code.co_name, file_hash=_hash_containing_file(code.co_filename), closure_hash=closure_hash, ) ``` Summary The PR is fundamentally correct in its approach. Update the ValueError handling to prevent the whole hash generation from aborting. Patch id() to prioritize actual object hashing for remote cache determinism. Drop these updates in, and from an engineering perspective, this is a beautiful fix to a nasty bug. Great job tracking this down!

### 🐛 Describe the bug

I caught this bug when implementing GGUF dequant in torch. I've started related discussions at https://github.com/city96/ComfyUI-GGUF/issues/405 and https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/issues/40070 . I've tried my best to make a minimal reproducer:
```python
import torch

def generate_blocks_bf16(n_blocks):
    data = torch.zeros((n_blocks, 2), dtype=torch.uint8)
    data[:, 0] = 0x80
    data[:, 1] = 0x3F
    return data

def generate_blocks_Q6_K(n_blocks):
    data = torch.zeros((n_blocks, 210), dtype=torch.uint8)
    data[:, 192:208] = 1
    data[:, 208] = 0x00
    data[:, 209] = 0x3C
    return data

def dequantize_blocks_BF16(blocks, dtype):
    return (blocks.view(torch.int16).to(torch.int32) << 16).view(torch.float32)

def split_block_dims(blocks, *args):
    n_max = blocks.shape[1]
    dims = list(args) + [n_max - sum(args)]
    xs = torch.split(blocks, dims, dim=1)
    return xs

def view_float16(x):
    return x.view(torch.float16)

def dequantize_blocks_Q6_K(blocks, dtype):
    QK_K = 256
    (ql, qh, scales, d) = split_block_dims(blocks, QK_K // 2, QK_K // 4, QK_K // 16)

    scales = scales.view(torch.int8).to(dtype)
    d = view_float16(d).to(dtype)
    d = d * scales

    n_blocks = blocks.shape[0]
    ql = ql.reshape((n_blocks, -1, 1, 64))

    return d

def wrap_compile(func):
    @torch.compile
    def _func(blocks, dtype):
        return func(blocks, dtype)

    return _func

dequantize_blocks_BF16_compiled = wrap_compile(dequantize_blocks_BF16)
dequantize_blocks_Q6_K_compiled = wrap_compile(dequantize_blocks_Q6_K)

device = "cpu"
n_blocks = 32

blocks_bf16 = generate_blocks_bf16(n_blocks).to(device)
blocks_Q6_K = generate_blocks_Q6_K(n_blocks).to(device)

out_bf16 = dequantize_blocks_BF16(blocks_bf16, torch.float32)
print("BF16 mean", out_bf16.mean().item())

out_Q6_K = dequantize_blocks_Q6_K(blocks_Q6_K, torch.float32)
print("Q6_K mean", out_Q6_K.mean().item())

out_bf16_compiled = dequantize_blocks_BF16_compiled(blocks_bf16, torch.float32)
print("BF16 mean compiled", out_bf16_compiled.mean().item())

out_Q6_K_compiled = dequantize_blocks_Q6_K_compiled(blocks_Q6_K, torch.float32)
print("Q6_K mean compiled", out_Q6_K_compiled.mean().item())
```
To pass the test, "Q6_K mean" should be the same as "Q6_K mean compiled". When the test fails, the output is like
```
BF16 mean 1.0
Q6_K mean 1.0
BF16 mean compiled 1.0
Q6_K mean compiled 0.0625
``` 
It fails on both CPU and CUDA.

Interestingly, if I comment out `out_bf16_compiled = dequantize_blocks_BF16_compiled(blocks_bf16, torch.float32)`, then the test passes.

Although `ql = ql.reshape((n_blocks, -1, 1, 64))` does not affect `d`, if I comment out it, the test passes.

I guess there is some undefined behavior like out-of-bounds memory access when we call `view(dtype)` and the number of bytes of the element changes.

Log with `TORCH_TRACE`: [dedicated_log_torch_trace_gox8spt4.log](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/24696736/dedicated_log_torch_trace_gox8spt4.log)

### Error logs

No error. It silently gives wrong numbers or nan.

Seq Faults after update [gfx1151]

### 🐛 Describe the bug

About two weeks ago I updated pytorch with the nightly build that I usually do every week or two. My system was working fine, not a single issue besides the one-off quirks you usually see. But after the update, I found that ComfyUI was failing to load any models. At first I thought it was the ComfyUI update that broke it, so I started there, but couldn't find any issue. The only message it was giving me was a seg fault when trying to load the model. I then turned to PyTorch and found that it would seg fault during a basic torch command.

```
import torch
torch.rand(50000,30000).cuda() @ torch.rand(30000,20000).cuda()
Segmentation fault         (core dumped) python
```


I've provided the valgrind, rocminfo, and boot entries.

Another odd thing is that rewinding the version, doesn't seem to fix the issue. I went back as far as a month and I got the exact same seg fault.

Another thing I should mention is that I did do a system update just before updating pytorch, so it could be possible that this could have happened from an AMD driver update and looking in the wrong spot. If I was smart, I would have tested torch after doing the system update before updating torch, but I have done this so many times, that I got used to it just working.

### 🐛 Describe the bug

When we run `dist.all_reduce` with `async_op=False` it should always return None. However torch.compile seems to be interpreting the output as `torch.Tensor`

```python
# save as: test_all_reduce_return.py
import os

import torch
import torch.distributed as dist


def init_dist():
    rank = int(os.environ["RANK"])
    world_size = int(os.environ["WORLD_SIZE"])
    dist.init_process_group(backend="gloo", rank=rank, world_size=world_size)
    return rank, world_size


def ar():
    x = torch.ones(1)
    w = dist.all_reduce(x, op=dist.ReduceOp.SUM, async_op=False)
    if w is None:
        print("W IS NONE")
        x += 1
    else:
        print("W IS NOT NONE")
        w.wait()
    return w, x


def main():
    rank, _ = init_dist()
    # Compiled: async_op=False should still return None
    compiled_ar = torch.compile(ar)
    w0, x0 = ar()
    print(w0, x0)
    try:
        w1, x1 = compiled_ar()
        print(f"[rank {rank}] compiled async_op=False: work={w1}  (is None? {w1 is None}), x1={x1.item()}")
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"[rank {rank}] compiled async_op=False: EXCEPTION: {type(e).__name__}: {e}")

    dist.barrier()
    dist.destroy_process_group()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

btw @thisisatharva-rh, is there a way to do all_reduce asynchronously, while also supporting `torch.compile(fullgraph=True)`?
```python

torch.distributed._functional_collectives.all_reduce
```
@KareemMusleh hey, that's not currently supported. `async_op=True` explicitly causes a graph break and isn't traceable.

Dynamo rewrites your dist.all_reduce into [dist._functional_collectives.all_reduce](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/bedb3e9047e9ad7130b73decd314732847a16ff0/torch/distributed/_functional_collectives.py#L154). So the output will be changed under the hood to a AsyncCollectiveTensor.

We don't support branching on the type of the old dist.all_reduce handle. You need to branch your eager logic and compile logic if you want to do that, using is_compiling(). A simpler option is to use the functional collective api in eager as well.

it's also good to note that when you compile with async_op=False, it will desugar to 

out_t = <collective>
...
out_t_waited = wait_tensor(out_t)

where wait_tensor is dropped as far as possible (i.e., before the first read)

---

> is there a way to do all_reduce asynchronously

> where wait_tensor is dropped as far as possible

This doesn't seem to be correct. Or maybe I'm misunderstanding something. [_maybe_wrap_tensor](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/bedb3e9047e9ad7130b73decd314732847a16ff0/torch/distributed/_functional_collectives.py#L1321) is called after the all_reduce collective is issued and it seems to run `wait_tensor` if it's compiling

When tracing, wait_tensor will appear right after the collective for the dynamo and aot graphs. But in inductor, there's some passes that will move wait_tensor closer to its consumer, effectively dropping it as far as possible. If you're not using inductor backend, you can write your own pass to delay them.

    gemm_out = torch.mm(weight, weight.T)

import os
import torch

torch._inductor.config.aten_distributed_optimizations.enable_overlap_scheduling = True
torch._inductor.config.aten_distributed_optimizations.collective_bucketing = True
torch._inductor.config.aten_distributed_optimizations.insert_overlap_deps = True

import torch.distributed as dist
from torch.distributed._functional_collectives import all_reduce

os.environ.setdefault("MASTER_ADDR", "localhost")
os.environ.setdefault("MASTER_PORT", "29500")

torch._logging.set_logs(output_code=True)


if dist.is_initialized():
    dist.destroy_process_group()

def init_dist():
    rank = int(os.environ.get("RANK", 0))
    world_size = int(os.environ.get("WORLD_SIZE", 1))
    if  rank == 0:
        dist.init_process_group(backend="fake", rank=rank, world_size=world_size)
    return rank, world_size

def overlap_collective_with_gemm(x, weight):
    """
    Pattern: all_reduce -> GEMM -> wait_tensor
    We want wait_tensor to stay AFTER the GEMM post-compile.
    """
    # Start async all_reduce (returns AsyncCollectiveTensor)
    x_reduced = all_reduce(x, reduceOp="sum", group=dist.group.WORLD)

    # GEMM that doesn't depend on all_reduce result
    gemm_out = torch.mm(weight, weight.T)

    return x_reduced + gemm_out.sum()

def check_wait_tensor_placement(gm):
    """Verify wait_tensor comes after mm in the graph."""
    print("\n=== FX Graph ===")
    gm.graph.print_tabular()

    mm_seen = False
    wait_seen = False
    order_correct = False

    for node in gm.graph.nodes:
        target_name = str(node.target)
        if "mm" in target_name.lower():
            mm_seen = True
            print(f"Found MM: {node.name}")
        if "wait_tensor" in target_name:
            wait_seen = True
            print(f"Found wait_tensor: {node.name}")
            if mm_seen:
                order_correct = True

    print(f"\n=== Result ===")
    print(f"MM found: {mm_seen}")
    print(f"wait_tensor found: {wait_seen}")
    print(f"wait_tensor AFTER mm: {order_correct}")
    return order_correct

def debug_backend(gm, example_inputs):
    """Custom backend that inspects the graph."""
    check_wait_tensor_placement(gm)
    return gm.forward

def main():
    rank, world_size = init_dist()
    try:
        device = torch.device(f"cuda:{rank}" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")

        # Test inputs
        x = torch.randn(64, 64, device=device)
        weight = torch.randn(128, 128, device=device)

        print("=== Eager execution ===")
        if world_size > 1:
            eager_out = overlap_collective_with_gemm(x.clone(), weight)
            print(f"Eager output: {eager_out.shape}")

        # print("\n=== Compiled (debug backend) ===")

        print("\n=== Compiled (inductor) with TORCH_LOGS ===")

        compiled_inductor = torch.compile(
            overlap_collective_with_gemm,
            backend="inductor",
            fullgraph=True,
            mode='max-autotune-no-cudagraphs'
        )

        if rank == 0:
            out = compiled_inductor(x.clone(), weight)
            print(f"Inductor output: {out.shape}")
    finally:
        dist.destroy_process_group()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

xmfan (member):Dynamo rewrites your dist.all_reduce into [dist._functional_collectives.all_reduce](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/bedb3e9047e9ad7130b73decd314732847a16ff0/torch/distributed/_functional_collectives.py#L154). So the output will be changed under the hood to a AsyncCollectiveTensor. We don't support branching on the type of the old dist.all_reduce handle. You need to branch your eager logic and compile logic if you want to do that, using is_compiling(). A simpler option is to use the functional collective api in eager as well.

### 🐛 Describe the bug

When we run `dist.all_reduce` with `async_op=False` it should always return None. However torch.compile seems to be interpreting the output as `torch.Tensor`

```python
# save as: test_all_reduce_return.py
import os

import torch
import torch.distributed as dist


def init_dist():
    rank = int(os.environ["RANK"])
    world_size = int(os.environ["WORLD_SIZE"])
    dist.init_process_group(backend="gloo", rank=rank, world_size=world_size)
    return rank, world_size


def ar():
    x = torch.ones(1)
    w = dist.all_reduce(x, op=dist.ReduceOp.SUM, async_op=False)
    if w is None:
        print("W IS NONE")
        x += 1
    else:
        print("W IS NOT NONE")
        w.wait()
    return w, x


def main():
    rank, _ = init_dist()
    # Compiled: async_op=False should still return None
    compiled_ar = torch.compile(ar)
    w0, x0 = ar()
    print(w0, x0)
    try:
        w1, x1 = compiled_ar()
        print(f"[rank {rank}] compiled async_op=False: work={w1}  (is None? {w1 is None}), x1={x1.item()}")
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"[rank {rank}] compiled async_op=False: EXCEPTION: {type(e).__name__}: {e}")

    dist.barrier()
    dist.destroy_process_group()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

My clang version is 18.1.3 and `nvcc --version`
```

Built on Tue_May_27_02:21:03_PDT_2025
Cuda compilation tools, release 12.9, V12.9.86
Build cuda_12.9.r12.9/compiler.36037853_0

```

```

One of the commenters in the stack overflow post stated that
> The extra parts in the symbol are typically related to GPU side CUDA ABI attributes

I am currently unable to finish building torch because `libtorch_cpu.so` doesn't produce all the mangled symbols expected by `libtorch_cuda.so`. Any help being able to finish building torch would be incredible

test_pre_quantized_model

Summary:
The error:
                                 
  assert config.version == 2, f"Unexpected version: {config.version}"         
  AssertionError: Unexpected version: 1                                       
                                                                              
  The model drisspg/fp8-opt-125m was quantized with an older torchao that used
   float8 config version 1, but the torchao version in your torch 2.11 image
  expects version 2. This is a breaking change in torchao's
  _float8_dynamic_activation_float8_weight_quantize_tensor.

  The flow is:
  1. TorchAOConfig.from_config detects is_checkpoint_torchao_serialized = True
   (the model has quant_method: torchao)
  2. During create_weights, it calls torchao_quantize_param_data → quantize_()
   to pre-quantize weights
  3. torchao's quantize_() hits the version assertion because the model's
  config is v1

  This isn't something fixable in vllm — the model checkpoint itself is
  incompatible with the newer torchao. The options are:

  1. Re-quantize the model with the new torchao and push an updated
  drisspg/fp8-opt-125m
  2. Skip the test for this torch version (if this is a CI concern)
  3. Use a different fp8 test model that was quantized with the newer torchao

  Bug: When using pytorch/gemma-3-27b-it-INT4 (Gemma 3) with a transformers v4 version that doesn't have full_attention/sliding_attention
  in ALLOWED_LAYER_TYPES, the nested rope_parameters dict isn't recognized as nested. The code then tries to validate the outer dict
  directly (which has layer type keys, not rope_type), causing "rope_parameters should have a 'rope_type' key".

Summary:
The error:
                                 
  assert config.version == 2, f"Unexpected version: {config.version}"         
  AssertionError: Unexpected version: 1                                       
                                                                              
  The model drisspg/fp8-opt-125m was quantized with an older torchao that used
   float8 config version 1, but the torchao version in your torch 2.11 image
  expects version 2. This is a breaking change in torchao's
  _float8_dynamic_activation_float8_weight_quantize_tensor.

  The flow is:
  1. TorchAOConfig.from_config detects is_checkpoint_torchao_serialized = True
   (the model has quant_method: torchao)
  2. During create_weights, it calls torchao_quantize_param_data → quantize_()
   to pre-quantize weights
  3. torchao's quantize_() hits the version assertion because the model's
  config is v1

  This isn't something fixable in vllm — the model checkpoint itself is
  incompatible with the newer torchao. The options are:

  1. Re-quantize the model with the new torchao and push an updated
  drisspg/fp8-opt-125m
  2. Skip the test for this torch version (if this is a CI concern)
  3. Use a different fp8 test model that was quantized with the newer torchao

[RFC] Enable Copy Engine all-gather in FSDP

### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

### Motivation
- Saves SM
- Reduces interference with the overlapping computation (e.g. GEMM)
- Micro benchmark https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/172714 showed 15% end-to-end speedup when the all-gather is overlapped with GEMM, compared to non-CE case.

### Recipe
- Allocate all-gather buffer from symmetric memory
- Init NCCL with zero-CTA policy

### Alternatives

_No response_

### Additional context

_No response_

cc @awgu @wanchaol @fegin @fduwjj @wz337 @wconstab @d4l3k @pragupta @msaroufim @dcci @aditvenk @xmfan @zhaojuanmao @mrshenli @rohan-varma @chauhang @mori360 @ppwwyyxx
Cc @weifengpy
Is there an existing recipe for copy engine collectives? I think we should be enabling this in our prefetching compiler passes as well.

> Is there an existing recipe for copy engine collectives?

the symmetric memory infrastructure already has the building blocks, the NCCL backend supports one-sided Put/Signal/Wait APIs (NCCL >= 2.29), LSA kernels for direct P2P copies, and the recent NVSHMEM backend provides an alternative path. What's missing is wiring these into FSDP's collective path with zero-CTA NCCL configuration.

FSDP2's Comm interface is already designed for this i.e., `AllGather.allocate()` is pluggable, so we can create a symmetric-memory-backed allocator that calls `torch.distributed._symmetric_memory.empty()` instead of `torch.empty()`. The actual all-gather call in `foreach_all_gather` would then operate on symm_mem-registered buffers, allowing NCCL to use copy engines with zero-CTA policy. The existing stream/event synchronization (copy-in stream -> all-gather stream -> copy-out) should work as-is

> we should be enabling this in our prefetching compiler passes as well.

Yes, FSDP's forward/backward prefetching already issues all-gathers early (`_prefetch_unshard`). A compiler pass could identify these prefetched all-gathers as candidates for copy engine offload, since they're specifically designed to overlap with compute. This is where the SM savings would have the most impact — prefetched all-gathers running on copy engines won't steal SMs from the GEMMs they're overlapping with.


happy to drive the further implementation here. 😄 

cc: @kwen2501

@kwen2501 @RohitRathore1 is this continuing the work from https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/170265 ? is this also possible for reduce-scatter? 

I have some time on fsdp now. I don't know if things change since last time.  cc @dzmitry-huba

@weifengpy this builds on the primitives validated in #170265, but isn't a direct continuation, #170265 was test-only with no FSDP integration as per understanding. This PR wires those symmetric memory primitives into FSDP2's pluggable `Comm` interface via `CopyEngineAllGather` and `set_copy_engine_all_gather()` on FSDPModule.

Reduce-scatter is definitely possible as a follow-up, the ReduceScatter interface has the same `allocate()` hook, so a `CopyEngineReduceScatter` would follow the same pattern. Would love to collaborate!
curious to see benchmark numbers on this once it is implemented :)

PR'ed here: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/176613
Would appreciate your review! Thanks in advance!

> [@xmfan](https://github.com/xmfan) Recipe here: [#170265](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/170265), basically using symmetric memory for all-gather buffer. Micro benchmark here [#172714](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/172714), looking at E2E speedup when overlapped with GEMM, saw 15% speedup.

awesome, thanks for the benchmark!

### 🐛 Describe the bug

Repro:
```
import torch

t0 = torch.tensor([84.3125], dtype=torch.float64).reshape((1,)).to(torch.float16).to("cuda:0")
t1 = torch.tensor([21.078125], dtype=torch.float64).reshape((1,)).to(torch.float16).to("cuda:0")

# Eager
eager_out = torch.floor_divide(t0, t1)

# Compiled
torch._dynamo.reset()
def fn(t0, t1):
    return torch.floor_divide(t0, t1)

compiled_fn = torch.compile(fn, fullgraph=True)
compiled_out = compiled_fn(t0, t1)

# Compare
print('eager  :', eager_out)
print('compiled:', compiled_out)
print('equal  :', torch.equal(eager_out, compiled_out))
if eager_out.is_floating_point():
    diff = (eager_out.to(torch.float64) - compiled_out.to(torch.float64)).abs()

```

Why does register_replacement not support fuzzy matching for optional parameters in operators when using search_fn or search_fn_pattern?

I am attempting to write a pattern matcher to match fused operators, and currently encounter an issue: neither search_fn nor search_fn_pattern provides a way to perform fuzzy matching for optional parameters. For example, optional parameters like offset and bias in the following operator prototype appear differently in the FX graph when they are passed or omitted:

Operator prototype as follows:
``` 
npu_quant_matmul(x1, x2, scale, *, offset=None, pertoken_scale=None, bias=None) -> Tensor
``` 


**Case 1 (with optional parameters):**
torch.ops.npu.npu_quant_matmul.default(arg2_1, arg3_1, arg4_1, offset=arg5_1, bias=arg6_1);
**Case 2 (without optional parameters):**
torch.ops.npu.npu_quant_matmul.default(arg2_1, arg3_1, arg4_1);
**Attempt 1: Using search_fn**
The following search_fn only matches Case 1 and fails to match Case 2 (where optional parameters are omitted). **To cover Case 2, I have to write a separate search_fn:**
``` 
# Only matches Case 1
def search_fn(x1, x2, scale, offset, bias):
    trans = x2.transpose(0, 1)
    return torch.ops.npu.npu_quant_matmul.default(x1, trans, scale, offset=offset, bias=bias)

# Only matches Case 2
def search_fn(x1, x2, scale):
    trans = x2.transpose(0, 1)
    return torch.ops.npu.npu_quant_matmul.default(x1, trans, scale)
```

**Attempt 2: Using search_fn_pattern (CallFunction)**
I also tried using search_fn_pattern (from torch._inductor.pattern_matcher import register_replacement as register) and wrote a CallFunction as shown below. However, using Ignored() results in a placeholder *, which causes a failure during the matching process when verifying len(self.args)!=len(node.args). It seems impossible to match both cases with a single CallFunction:
```
def _build_search_pattern():
        npu_transpose_func = CallFunction(
            torch.ops.aten.transpose.int, 
            KeywordArg("x2"), 
            Ignored(), 
            Ignored(), 
            _users=1
        )

        output = CallFunction(
            torch.ops.npu.npu_quant_matmul.default, 
            KeywordArg("x1"),
            npu_transpose_func,
            KeywordArg('scale'),
            offset=KeywordArg('offset'), #Alternatively, writing Ignore() here will cause a failure during the matching process when verifying that len(self.args)!=len(node.args)
            bias=KeywordArg('bias'), 
            _users=1
        )

        return output
```

**Impact:**
Some operators may have more optional parameters (e.g., n optional parameters). In such cases, I would need to write 2ⁿ search_fn or search_fn_pattern to cover all scenarios, which is extremely inefficient and unscalable.
**Questions:**
1. Is there any syntax to perform fuzzy matching for this scenario, so that both cases (with/without optional parameters passed) can be matched with a single pattern?
2. What is the difference between the two writing methods in the matching process:
    1.CallFunction(offset=KeywordArg('offset'))
    2.CallFunction(KeywordArg('offset'))?

input_vector.body:
I am attempting to write a pattern matcher to match fused operators, and currently encounter an issue: neither search_fn nor search_fn_pattern provides a way to perform fuzzy matching for optional parameters. For example, optional parameters like offset and bias in the following operator prototype appear differently in the FX graph when they are passed or omitted:

Operator prototype as follows:
``` 
npu_quant_matmul(x1, x2, scale, *, offset=None, pertoken_scale=None, bias=None) -> Tensor
``` 


**Case 1 (with optional parameters):**
torch.ops.npu.npu_quant_matmul.default(arg2_1, arg3_1, arg4_1, offset=arg5_1, bias=arg6_1);
**Case 2 (without optional parameters):**
torch.ops.npu.npu_quant_matmul.default(arg2_1, arg3_1, arg4_1);
**Attempt 1: Using search_fn**
The following search_fn only matches Case 1 and fails to match Case 2 (where optional parameters are omitted). **To cover Case 2, I have to write a separate search_fn:**
``` 
# Only matches Case 1
def search_fn(x1, x2, scale, offset, bias):
    trans = x2.transpose(0, 1)
    return torch.ops.npu.npu_quant_matmul.default(x1, trans, scale, offset=offset, bias=bias)

# Only matches Case 2
def search_fn(x1, x2, scale):
    trans = x2.transpose(0, 1)
    return torch.ops.npu.npu_quant_matmul.default(x1, trans, scale)
```

**Attempt 2: Using search_fn_pattern (CallFunction)**
I also tried using search_fn_pattern (from torch._inductor.pattern_matcher import register_replacement as register) and wrote a CallFunction as shown below. However, using Ignored() results in a placeholder *, which causes a failure during the matching process when verifying len(self.args)!=len(node.args). It seems impossible to match both cases with a single CallFunction:
```
def _build_search_pattern():
        npu_transpose_func = CallFunction(
            torch.ops.aten.transpose.int, 
            KeywordArg("x2"), 
            Ignored(), 
            Ignored(), 
            _users=1
        )

        output = CallFunction(
            torch.ops.npu.npu_quant_matmul.default, 
            KeywordArg("x1"),
            npu_transpose_func,
            KeywordArg('scale'),
            offset=KeywordArg('offset'), #Alternatively, writing Ignore() here will cause a failure during the matching process when verifying that len(self.args)!=len(node.args)
            bias=KeywordArg('bias'), 
            _users=1
        )

        return output
```

**Impact:**
Some operators may have more optional parameters (e.g., n optional parameters). In such cases, I would need to write 2ⁿ search_fn or search_fn_pattern to cover all scenarios, which is extremely inefficient and unscalable.
**Questions:**
1. Is there any syntax to perform fuzzy matching for this scenario, so that both cases (with/without optional parameters passed) can be matched with a single pattern?
2. What is the difference between the two writing methods in the matching process:
    1.CallFunction(offset=KeywordArg('offset'))
    2.CallFunction(KeywordArg('offset'))?

When using the cuDNN backend, custom masks become ineffective.

### 🐛 Describe the bug

In PyTorch's SDPA implementation, when using different backends, custom masks don't seem to take effect.

The test compared two backends: SDPBackend.MATH and SDPBackend.CUDNN_ATTENTION.

```
import torch
from torch.nn.attention import SDPBackend, sdpa_kernel

torch.set_printoptions(sci_mode=False, precision=4)

def calc_and_print(q: torch.Tensor, k: torch.Tensor, v: torch.Tensor, attention_mask: torch.Tensor):
    with sdpa_kernel(SDPBackend.MATH):
        attn_output_math = torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention(
            query=q.transpose(1, 2),
            key=k.transpose(1, 2),
            value=v.transpose(1, 2),
            attn_mask=attention_mask,
            is_causal=False,
            enable_gqa=True,
        )
    with sdpa_kernel(SDPBackend.CUDNN_ATTENTION):
        attn_output_cudnn = torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention(
            query=q.transpose(1, 2),
            key=k.transpose(1, 2),
            value=v.transpose(1, 2),
            attn_mask=attention_mask,
            is_causal=False,
            enable_gqa=True,
        )
    return attn_output_math, attn_output_cudnn

q = torch.randn(1, 10, 8, 8).to("cuda").bfloat16()
k = torch.randn(1, 10, 1, 8).to("cuda").bfloat16()
v = torch.randn(1, 10, 1, 8).to("cuda").bfloat16()

attention_mask_custom = torch.zeros(10, 10, dtype=torch.bool).to("cuda")
attention_mask_custom[:7, :7] = torch.tril(torch.ones(7, 7, dtype=torch.bool), diagonal=0)
attention_mask_full = torch.tril(torch.ones(10, 10, dtype=torch.bool), diagonal=0).to("cuda")

print(f"attention_mask_custom:\n{attention_mask_custom}")
custom_math, custom_cudnn = calc_and_print(q, k, v, attention_mask_custom)
print(f"custom_math:\n{custom_math[0,0]}")
print(f"custom_cudnn:\n{custom_cudnn[0,0]}")

print("="*40)

print(f"attention_mask_full:\n{attention_mask_full}")
full_math, full_cudnn = calc_and_print(q, k, v, attention_mask_full)
print(f"full_math:\n{full_math[0,0]}")
print(f"full_cudnn:\n{full_cudnn[0,0]}")

print("="*40)

cudnn_diff_between_custom_and_full = custom_cudnn - full_cudnn
print(f"cudnn_diff_between_custom_and_full:\n{cudnn_diff_between_custom_and_full[0,0]}")
```

### 🐛 Describe the bug

In PyTorch's SDPA implementation, when using different backends, custom masks don't seem to take effect.

The test compared two backends: SDPBackend.MATH and SDPBackend.CUDNN_ATTENTION.

```
import torch
from torch.nn.attention import SDPBackend, sdpa_kernel

torch.set_printoptions(sci_mode=False, precision=4)

def calc_and_print(q: torch.Tensor, k: torch.Tensor, v: torch.Tensor, attention_mask: torch.Tensor):
    with sdpa_kernel(SDPBackend.MATH):
        attn_output_math = torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention(
            query=q.transpose(1, 2),
            key=k.transpose(1, 2),
            value=v.transpose(1, 2),
            attn_mask=attention_mask,
            is_causal=False,
            enable_gqa=True,
        )
    with sdpa_kernel(SDPBackend.CUDNN_ATTENTION):
        attn_output_cudnn = torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention(
            query=q.transpose(1, 2),
            key=k.transpose(1, 2),
            value=v.transpose(1, 2),
            attn_mask=attention_mask,
            is_causal=False,
            enable_gqa=True,
        )
    return attn_output_math, attn_output_cudnn

q = torch.randn(1, 10, 8, 8).to("cuda").bfloat16()
k = torch.randn(1, 10, 1, 8).to("cuda").bfloat16()
v = torch.randn(1, 10, 1, 8).to("cuda").bfloat16()

attention_mask_custom = torch.zeros(10, 10, dtype=torch.bool).to("cuda")
attention_mask_custom[:7, :7] = torch.tril(torch.ones(7, 7, dtype=torch.bool), diagonal=0)
attention_mask_full = torch.tril(torch.ones(10, 10, dtype=torch.bool), diagonal=0).to("cuda")

print(f"attention_mask_custom:\n{attention_mask_custom}")
custom_math, custom_cudnn = calc_and_print(q, k, v, attention_mask_custom)
print(f"custom_math:\n{custom_math[0,0]}")
print(f"custom_cudnn:\n{custom_cudnn[0,0]}")

print("="*40)

print(f"attention_mask_full:\n{attention_mask_full}")
full_math, full_cudnn = calc_and_print(q, k, v, attention_mask_full)
print(f"full_math:\n{full_math[0,0]}")
print(f"full_cudnn:\n{full_cudnn[0,0]}")

print("="*40)

cudnn_diff_between_custom_and_full = custom_cudnn - full_cudnn
print(f"cudnn_diff_between_custom_and_full:\n{cudnn_diff_between_custom_and_full[0,0]}")
```

deliberation_thread.body:
nn.Parameter creation in FSDPParam crashes for non floating point tensors

### 🐛 Describe the bug

`FSDPParam._init_sharded_param()` (line 381) and `to_sharded_post_forward()` (line 546) in `torch/distributed/fsdp/_fully_shard/_fsdp_param.py` create `nn.Parameter` without passing `requires_grad`, defaulting to `True`. For non-floating-point tensors (e.g. uint8), this crashes:
```
RuntimeError: only Tensors of floating point dtype can require gradients
```

The intended fix is already present on line 382 and line 501, already correctly passes `requires_grad`:
```python
# Line 501 (correct)
self._unsharded_param = nn.Parameter(
    unsharded_param, requires_grad=self.sharded_param.requires_grad
)

# Line 381 (crashes before line 382 fixup)
self.sharded_param = nn.Parameter(self.to_sharded_dtensor(sharded_param))
self.sharded_param.requires_grad_(param.requires_grad)

# Line 546 (no fixup at all)
self._sharded_post_forward_param = nn.Parameter(
    self.to_sharded_post_forward_dtensor(sharded_post_forward_tensor)
)
```

The fix is to pass `requires_grad` at creation time, consistent with line 501:
```python
# Line 381
self.sharded_param = nn.Parameter(
    self.to_sharded_dtensor(sharded_param),
    requires_grad=param.requires_grad,
)

# Line 546
self._sharded_post_forward_param = nn.Parameter(
    self.to_sharded_post_forward_dtensor(sharded_post_forward_tensor),
    requires_grad=self.sharded_param.requires_grad,
)
```

Are you trying to use FSDP for inference mode?

For training, autograd doesn't support uint8, but more generally, derivatives require continuous functions over continuous domains, ints are discrete, so I'm not sure how you would define differentiation. If this is about quantization, you shouldn't declare your weights directly as torch.uint8, take a look at https://github.com/pytorch/ao.

@xmfan 
Thanks for the response! To clarify, this is not about computing gradients on uint8 tensors.
The parameter in question is frozen (`requires_grad=False`), such as a quantized base weight in QLoRA. The issue is that `nn.Parameter(data)` defaults to `requires_grad=True` at creation time, which crashes for non-float dtypes before the next line can set it back to `False`:
```python
# Line 381: crashes at creation because default requires_grad=True
self.sharded_param = nn.Parameter(self.to_sharded_dtensor(sharded_param))
# Line 382: never reached
self.sharded_param.requires_grad_(param.requires_grad)  # would set False
```

The fix is simply passing the original `requires_grad` to the constructor, which is already done correctly on line 501:
```python
# Line 501 (already correct pattern)
self._unsharded_param = nn.Parameter(
    unsharded_param, requires_grad=self.sharded_param.requires_grad
)
```

This doesn't enable gradient computation on uint8. It prevents the constructor from trying to enable it when it shouldn't.

thanks for the report. I drafted a fix: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/177948
also need to take care of mixed precision for non-float dtypes

For training, autograd doesn't support uint8, but more generally, derivatives require continuous functions over continuous domains, ints are discrete, so I'm not sure how you would define differentiation. roycho96 (external):@xmfan Thanks for the response! To clarify, this is not about computing gradients on uint8 tensors. The parameter in question is frozen (`requires_grad=False`), such as a quantized base weight in QLoRA. The issue is that `nn.Parameter(data)` defaults to `requires_grad=True` at creation time, which crashes for non-float dtypes before the next line can set it back to `False`: ```python # Line 381: crashes at creation because default requires_grad=True self.sharded_param = nn.Parameter(self.to_sharded_dtensor(sharded_param)) # Line 382: never reached self.sharded_param.requires_grad_(param.requires_grad) # would set False ``` The fix is simply passing the original `requires_grad` to the constructor, which is already done correctly on line 501: ```python # Line 501 (already correct pattern) self._unsharded_param = nn.Parameter( unsharded_param, requires_grad=self.sharded_param.requires_grad ) ``` This doesn't enable gradient computation on uint8. It prevents the constructor from trying to enable it when it shouldn't.

### 🐛 Describe the bug

`FSDPParam._init_sharded_param()` (line 381) and `to_sharded_post_forward()` (line 546) in `torch/distributed/fsdp/_fully_shard/_fsdp_param.py` create `nn.Parameter` without passing `requires_grad`, defaulting to `True`. For non-floating-point tensors (e.g. uint8), this crashes:
```
RuntimeError: only Tensors of floating point dtype can require gradients
```

The intended fix is already present on line 382 and line 501, already correctly passes `requires_grad`:
```python
# Line 501 (correct)
self._unsharded_param = nn.Parameter(
    unsharded_param, requires_grad=self.sharded_param.requires_grad
)

# Line 381 (crashes before line 382 fixup)
self.sharded_param = nn.Parameter(self.to_sharded_dtensor(sharded_param))
self.sharded_param.requires_grad_(param.requires_grad)

# Line 546 (no fixup at all)
self._sharded_post_forward_param = nn.Parameter(
    self.to_sharded_post_forward_dtensor(sharded_post_forward_tensor)
)
```

The fix is to pass `requires_grad` at creation time, consistent with line 501:
```python
# Line 381
self.sharded_param = nn.Parameter(
    self.to_sharded_dtensor(sharded_param),
    requires_grad=param.requires_grad,
)

# Line 546
self._sharded_post_forward_param = nn.Parameter(
    self.to_sharded_post_forward_dtensor(sharded_post_forward_tensor),
    requires_grad=self.sharded_param.requires_grad,
)
```

`torch.compile` crashes with FakeTensor view stride error on valid model with `index_put_` scatter

### 🐛 Describe the bug


`torch.compile` with `inductor` backend crashes during Dynamo tracing with a `ValueError: Cannot view a tensor with shape and strides` error when compiling a valid transformer model that uses `torch.index_put_` with `accumulate=True` (scatter-add pattern). The same model runs correctly in eager mode.

The error occurs because Dynamo's FakeTensor mode infers incorrect strides for the attention output tensor. When the model calls `attn_output.view(-1, self.hidden_dim)`, FakeTensor computes strides `(256, 1024, 1)` for shape `(4, 32, 256)`, making the `view` operation invalid. In eager mode, the actual tensor is contiguous with strides `(8192, 256, 1)`, so `view` succeeds.

This was discovered via a fuzzer-generated sparse gradient accumulation model targeting the `partitioned_scatter` Inductor optimization (reduced atomic contention for high-contention `index_put_`).

### Minimal reproducer

```python
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

class ScatterModel(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, vocab_size=5000, hidden_dim=256, num_heads=8):
        super().__init__()
        self.hidden_dim = hidden_dim
        self.embedding = nn.Embedding(vocab_size, hidden_dim)
        self.attention = nn.MultiheadAttention(hidden_dim, num_heads, batch_first=True)
        self.norm = nn.LayerNorm(hidden_dim)
        self.ffn = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(hidden_dim, hidden_dim * 4),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Linear(hidden_dim * 4, hidden_dim)
        )
        self.output_proj = nn.Linear(hidden_dim, vocab_size)
        self.register_buffer('buffer', torch.zeros(vocab_size, hidden_dim))

    def forward(self, input_ids):
        x = self.embedding(input_ids)
        attn_output, _ = self.attention(x, x, x)
        x = self.norm(x + attn_output)
        x = self.norm(x + self.ffn(x))
        logits = self.output_proj(x)

        # Scatter-add with high contention
        indices = input_ids.view(-1)
        values = attn_output.view(-1, self.hidden_dim)  # <-- Crashes here in compile
        buf = self.buffer.clone()
        torch.index_put_(buf, (indices,), values, accumulate=True)

        return F.softmax(logits, dim=-1), buf

device = "cuda"
model = ScatterModel().to(device).eval()
x = torch.randint(0, 5000, (4, 32), dtype=torch.long, device=device)

# Eager: works
with torch.no_grad():
    probs, buf = model(x)
print(f"Eager: OK, probs={probs.shape}, buf={buf.shape}")

# Compiled: crashes
torch._dynamo.reset()
compiled = torch.compile(model, backend="inductor")
try:
    with torch.no_grad():
        probs2, buf2 = compiled(x)
    print(f"Compiled: OK")
except Exception as e:
    print(f"Compiled: CRASH — {type(e).__name__}: {e}")
```

### Behavior summary

| Mode | Result |

### 🐛 Describe the bug


`torch.compile` with `inductor` backend crashes during Dynamo tracing with a `ValueError: Cannot view a tensor with shape and strides` error when compiling a valid transformer model that uses `torch.index_put_` with `accumulate=True` (scatter-add pattern). The same model runs correctly in eager mode.

The error occurs because Dynamo's FakeTensor mode infers incorrect strides for the attention output tensor. When the model calls `attn_output.view(-1, self.hidden_dim)`, FakeTensor computes strides `(256, 1024, 1)` for shape `(4, 32, 256)`, making the `view` operation invalid. In eager mode, the actual tensor is contiguous with strides `(8192, 256, 1)`, so `view` succeeds.

This was discovered via a fuzzer-generated sparse gradient accumulation model targeting the `partitioned_scatter` Inductor optimization (reduced atomic contention for high-contention `index_put_`).

### Minimal reproducer

```python
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

class ScatterModel(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, vocab_size=5000, hidden_dim=256, num_heads=8):
        super().__init__()
        self.hidden_dim = hidden_dim
        self.embedding = nn.Embedding(vocab_size, hidden_dim)
        self.attention = nn.MultiheadAttention(hidden_dim, num_heads, batch_first=True)
        self.norm = nn.LayerNorm(hidden_dim)
        self.ffn = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(hidden_dim, hidden_dim * 4),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Linear(hidden_dim * 4, hidden_dim)
        )
        self.output_proj = nn.Linear(hidden_dim, vocab_size)
        self.register_buffer('buffer', torch.zeros(vocab_size, hidden_dim))

    def forward(self, input_ids):
        x = self.embedding(input_ids)
        attn_output, _ = self.attention(x, x, x)
        x = self.norm(x + attn_output)
        x = self.norm(x + self.ffn(x))
        logits = self.output_proj(x)

        # Scatter-add with high contention
        indices = input_ids.view(-1)
        values = attn_output.view(-1, self.hidden_dim)  # <-- Crashes here in compile
        buf = self.buffer.clone()
        torch.index_put_(buf, (indices,), values, accumulate=True)

        return F.softmax(logits, dim=-1), buf

device = "cuda"
model = ScatterModel().to(device).eval()
x = torch.randint(0, 5000, (4, 32), dtype=torch.long, device=device)

# Eager: works
with torch.no_grad():
    probs, buf = model(x)
print(f"Eager: OK, probs={probs.shape}, buf={buf.shape}")

# Compiled: crashes
torch._dynamo.reset()
compiled = torch.compile(model, backend="inductor")
try:
    with torch.no_grad():
        probs2, buf2 = compiled(x)
    print(f"Compiled: OK")
except Exception as e:
    print(f"Compiled: CRASH — {type(e).__name__}: {e}")
```

### Behavior summary

| Mode | Result |
|------|--------|
| Eager |  Succeeds |
| `torch.compile(backend="inductor")` |  Crashes: `ValueError: Cannot view a tensor with shape torch.Size([4, 32, 256]) and strides (256, 1024, 1) as a tensor with shape (128, 256)!` |

### Root cause analysis

The error message reveals a stride mismatch in Dynamo's FakeTensor:

```
Cannot view a tensor with shape torch.Size([4, 32, 256]) and strides (256, 1024, 1)
as a tensor with shape (128, 256)!
```

- **Expected strides** (contiguous): `(8192, 256, 1)` — `4*32*256, 32*256, 1`
- **FakeTensor strides**: `(256, 1024, 1)` — incorrect, not contiguous

The `nn.MultiheadAttention` output tensor has correct contiguous strides in eager mode, but Dynamo's symbolic shape propagation / FakeTensor computes incorrect strides for the attention output, causing the subsequent `view(-1, hidden_dim)` to fail.

This is a Dynamo FakeTensor stride inference bug for `nn.MultiheadAttention` output tensors.


### Error logs

```
RuntimeError when making fake tensor call
  Explanation: Dynamo failed to run FX node with fake tensors:
    call_method view(*(FakeTensor(..., device='cuda:0', size=(4, 32, 256)), -1, 256), **{}):
    got ValueError('Cannot view a tensor with shape torch.Size([4, 32, 256]) and
    strides (256, 1024, 1) as a tensor with shape (128, 256)!')
  Hint: Your code may result in an error when running in eager.
    Please double check that your code doesn't contain a similar error when actually running eager/uncompiled
```

Note: The hint is misleading — eager mode works correctly because the actual tensor IS contiguous.

### Versions

```
PyTorch version: 2.12.0.dev20260315+cu126
Python: 3.10.12
OS: Ubuntu 22.04.5 LTS (WSL2)
GPU: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3060 Laptop GPU
CUDA: 12.6
```

[PERFORMANCE] [NN] Change `torch._C._get_tracing_state()` to `torch._C._is_tracing()` for around 15% improved performance of `module.py` `_call_impl()`

# Summary
This issue suggests replacing `torch._C._get_tracing_state()` with `torch._C._is_tracing()` in `torch/nn/modules/module.py` inside `_call_impl()`, avoiding unnecessary object overhead and leading to a performance boost by around 15% (see benchmark results down below).

# Explanation
In the original implementation of PyTorch we used `torch._C._get_tracing_state()` which returns a full tracing state object. For the purpose of checking whether tracing is active (and we do not use the object itself anymore later on), this is unnecessary overhead. Replacing it with `torch._C._is_tracing()` directly returns a boolean, avoiding usage of the object itself and instead only checking the returned boolean via `torch._C._is_tracing()`. The benchmark results (down below) confirm a ~15% performance improvement for `module.py` `_call_impl()`.

# Implementation and benchmarks
I've implemented the suggested change (see implementation) and tested it with the following scripts:

`torchcontroller.py`

# Summary
This issue suggests replacing `torch._C._get_tracing_state()` with `torch._C._is_tracing()` in `torch/nn/modules/module.py` inside `_call_impl()`, avoiding unnecessary object overhead and leading to a performance boost by around 15% (see benchmark results down below).

# Explanation
In the original implementation of PyTorch we used `torch._C._get_tracing_state()` which returns a full tracing state object. For the purpose of checking whether tracing is active (and we do not use the object itself anymore later on), this is unnecessary overhead. Replacing it with `torch._C._is_tracing()` directly returns a boolean, avoiding usage of the object itself and instead only checking the returned boolean via `torch._C._is_tracing()`. The benchmark results (down below) confirm a ~15% performance improvement for `module.py` `_call_impl()`.

torch.compile(dynamic=True) on CUDA gives large output mismatch vs eager for BatchNorm2d + Conv2d

### 🐛 Describe the bug

Summary: For a small module (BatchNorm2d(96) → Conv2d(96→256, k=5, p=2)), torch.compile(..., dynamic=True) on CUDA produces outputs that differ massively from eager mode when using the same weights and input. Max per-element relative error vs eager is ~1.7, while float-level agreement would be ~1e-7 or smaller.

Repro: Load fixed input.pt and state_dict subset (bn1.*, conv2.*), run .eval(), compare eager forward to torch.compile(..., dynamic=True) on the conv2 output (same x, same sd, two separate module instances).

Expected: Compiled forward matches eager within tight float tolerance.
Actual: Large relative error (~O(1)) between compiled and eager outputs.

```python
import os
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
_DIR = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
INPUT_PT = os.path.join(_DIR, "input.pt")
SD_PT = os.path.join(_DIR, "sd.pt")
THRESHOLD = 1.19e-7
DEVICE = torch.device("cuda")

class Bn1Conv2(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, sd: dict):
        super().__init__()
        self.bn1 = nn.BatchNorm2d(96)
        self.conv2 = nn.Conv2d(96, 256, kernel_size=5, padding=2, bias=True)
        self.load_state_dict(sd, strict=True)

    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        x = self.bn1(x)
        return self.conv2(x)

def main():
    x = torch.load(INPUT_PT, map_location="cpu").float()
    print(f"input min={x.min().item():.6g}  max={x.max().item():.6g}")
    x = x.to(DEVICE)
    sd = torch.load(SD_PT, map_location="cpu")
    wmin = float("inf")
    wmax = float("-inf")
    for v in sd.values():
        if torch.is_tensor(v):
            t = v.float().cpu()
            wmin = min(wmin, float(t.min().item()))
            wmax = max(wmax, float(t.max().item()))
    print(f"weights min={wmin:.6g}  max={wmax:.6g}")

    m0 = Bn1Conv2(sd).to(DEVICE).eval()
    with torch.no_grad():
        y0 = m0(x)

    m1 = torch.compile(Bn1Conv2(sd).to(DEVICE).eval(), dynamic=True)
    with torch.no_grad():
        y1 = m1(x)

    o = y0.detach().float().cpu().reshape(y0.shape[0], -1)
    s = y1.detach().float().cpu().reshape(y1.shape[0], -1)
    eps = 1e-12
    valid = torch.isfinite(o) & torch.isfinite(s)
    diff = torch.where(valid, (s - o).abs() / (o.abs() + eps), torch.zeros_like(o))
    per = diff.max(dim=1).values
    gmax = float(per.max().item())

    print("modes: eager  vs  torch.compile(dynamic=True)")
    print(
        f"relative error: max_rel={gmax:.6e}  "
        f"threshold={THRESHOLD:.2e}"
    )

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

```

### 🐛 Describe the bug

Summary: For a small module (BatchNorm2d(96) → Conv2d(96→256, k=5, p=2)), torch.compile(..., dynamic=True) on CUDA produces outputs that differ massively from eager mode when using the same weights and input. Max per-element relative error vs eager is ~1.7, while float-level agreement would be ~1e-7 or smaller.

Repro: Load fixed input.pt and state_dict subset (bn1.*, conv2.*), run .eval(), compare eager forward to torch.compile(..., dynamic=True) on the conv2 output (same x, same sd, two separate module instances).

Expected: Compiled forward matches eager within tight float tolerance.
Actual: Large relative error (~O(1)) between compiled and eager outputs.

```python
import os
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
_DIR = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
INPUT_PT = os.path.join(_DIR, "input.pt")
SD_PT = os.path.join(_DIR, "sd.pt")
THRESHOLD = 1.19e-7
DEVICE = torch.device("cuda")

class Bn1Conv2(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, sd: dict):
        super().__init__()
        self.bn1 = nn.BatchNorm2d(96)
        self.conv2 = nn.Conv2d(96, 256, kernel_size=5, padding=2, bias=True)
        self.load_state_dict(sd, strict=True)

    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        x = self.bn1(x)
        return self.conv2(x)

def main():
    x = torch.load(INPUT_PT, map_location="cpu").float()
    print(f"input min={x.min().item():.6g}  max={x.max().item():.6g}")
    x = x.to(DEVICE)
    sd = torch.load(SD_PT, map_location="cpu")
    wmin = float("inf")
    wmax = float("-inf")
    for v in sd.values():
        if torch.is_tensor(v):
            t = v.float().cpu()
            wmin = min(wmin, float(t.min().item()))
            wmax = max(wmax, float(t.max().item()))
    print(f"weights min={wmin:.6g}  max={wmax:.6g}")

    m0 = Bn1Conv2(sd).to(DEVICE).eval()
    with torch.no_grad():
        y0 = m0(x)

    m1 = torch.compile(Bn1Conv2(sd).to(DEVICE).eval(), dynamic=True)
    with torch.no_grad():
        y1 = m1(x)

    o = y0.detach().float().cpu().reshape(y0.shape[0], -1)
    s = y1.detach().float().cpu().reshape(y1.shape[0], -1)
    eps = 1e-12
    valid = torch.isfinite(o) & torch.isfinite(s)
    diff = torch.where(valid, (s - o).abs() / (o.abs() + eps), torch.zeros_like(o))
    per = diff.max(dim=1).values
    gmax = float(per.max().item())

    print("modes: eager  vs  torch.compile(dynamic=True)")
    print(
        f"relative error: max_rel={gmax:.6e}  "
        f"threshold={THRESHOLD:.2e}"
    )

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

```
